stories.title: The Doom Prophecy Warns Kamsa
stories.story:
On the day of his sister's wedding, Kamsa, the son of King Ugrasena of Mathura, did something no prince was expected to do. He climbed onto the wedding chariot and took the reins himself. Devaki was the youngest daughter of the house and the sister he loved, and he wanted to drive her and her new husband through the streets with his own hands. It was an act of affection, and everyone who watched the procession that day saw only a brother honouring his sister.

The procession was a river of gold. Four hundred elephants swayed beneath garlands of gold, and two hundred young maidservants, dressed and adorned in their finest, walked beside the chariot. Conches sounded and horns blew, and the deep roll of mridanga drums and kettledrums filled the air, so that the whole road seemed to move to a single bright rhythm. Vasudeva, the groom, sat beside his bride, and the road out of the city lay open and shining before them. It was the kind of day a family remembers for its brightness, its noise, its promise.

Then, on that open road, a voice spoke.

It had no body. It came from nowhere and everywhere at once, deep and rolling as thunder, and it was meant for Kamsa alone. No one else in the procession heard a thing; the drums and the conches played on for a few beats longer while the prince alone sat frozen with the words ringing in his ears. The voice called him a fool, and it told him that the woman he was driving would bear eight children, and that her eighth child would take away his life. The words were few, but they were enough to undo a man.

The music stopped. The elephants stood still. Kamsa's hands tightened on the reins, and for a long moment he did not move. Then, in a single motion, he reached for his sword and turned on his own sister, meaning to kill her there in the chariot, before any such child could ever be born.

Vasudeva moved first. He placed himself between the blade and his bride and would not step aside, and he reasoned with the prince until, slowly, the arm that held the sword came down.

The sword did not fall that day. But something else had already fallen. The brother who had held the reins out of love was gone, and in his place sat a man who would never again feel safe. A warning that named no crime of his own, only the child of his sister's womb, had turned his affection into fear. A shadow fell across the wedding gifts still gleaming on the road, across the garlands and the drums, across a day built for joy. The prophecy had been spoken, and it could not be unspoken. From that hour, every child born to Devaki would come into the world watched, and Kamsa would meet each one with the same cold dread that had risen in him on that bright road.
stories.reflection: The prophecy arrives at a moment of pure affection, a brother driving his sister to her wedding, and turns that affection into fear. Kamsa's tragedy does not begin with cruelty but with terror for his own life.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha tells this moment differently: there the warning is carried not by a bodiless voice but by the sage Narada, who travels to Mathura to tell Kamsa of his coming doom.
stories.content_note: Kamsa draws his sword on his sister; the violence is threatened but not carried out.
stories.next_story_tease: But the prophecy had already taken root, and Kamsa would spend years trying to keep Devaki's eighth child from ever drawing breath.
stories.hero_scene: Kamsa frozen in the wedding chariot, reins in hand, as a bodiless voice warns him of his doom; Vasudeva steps between him and a terrified Devaki while the gold-decked procession halts behind them.
stories.variant_notes: BP/VP: a bodiless heavenly voice warns at the wedding; HV: Narada delivers the warning. VP 5.1 also folds in the pacification beat.

stories.title: Krishna Is Born at Midnight
stories.story:
At the stroke of midnight, the world outside the prison began to change, and almost no one noticed. The dark lay over Mathura like a held breath, and then, very quietly, it began to give way.

In Mathura the night had been heavy, but now, slowly, the ten directions grew calm. The sky cleared of its clouds, and the stars rose in their hosts, bright and close. The rivers, stirred and clouded all day, settled until their water ran clear as glass, and the ponds put on their lotus flowers like ornaments laid out for a guest. The seas, far off, took up a low, melodious murmur, as if they too were singing. A wind rose that was gentle and cool to the touch, and it carried a clean, sweet scent, so that anyone awake at that hour would have breathed it in and wondered what had changed. Even the fires that had gone cold in the hearths of the city began, some said, to burn again with a mild and gentle flame. And a soft light spread over the whole earth, as though moonlight had been poured across it. And the minds of good people everywhere grew suddenly at peace, as though a long and private worry had lifted from them without their knowing why.

Inside the prison, none of this could be seen. The cell was small and dark, and in it Devaki lay waiting. She and Vasudeva had been shut away by her brother Kamsa, who now ruled Mathura and who lived in terror of a prophecy: that Devaki's eighth child would be his death. One by one he had killed the children she had borne before this one, dashing them as soon as they came into the world, so that no child could grow into the doom that had been promised to him. Each birth in that room had ended the same way, and still the child came.

The tradition remembers the hour itself as sacred, the night called Jayanti, the most blessed of the year, and the moment within it the most fortunate. Men who kept the count of such things named the star of that hour Abhijit, and the moment itself Vijaya, the victorious. The child came into the cell quietly, without trumpets or attendants. He came as quietly as the full moon that rises over the east of the world. But outside, where no one was watching, the whole of nature seemed to know. The kinnaras and the gandharvas sang, the siddhas and the charanas praised what was happening, and the sages and the gods, unseen, let fall showers of flowers from the sky. Somewhere above, a celestial bugle sounded, though no hand had struck it.

The hymns were not heard in the streets of Mathura. The city slept, and the king slept, and the guards kept their watch at the prison doors, unaware that the hour they had been set to guard against had already come. The only witnesses to that joy were the two prisoners in the cell and the quiet elements of the world.

No one in Mathura heard the singing. But something had entered the world that the wind, the rivers, and the stars all seemed to recognize, and the night itself had turned gentle to receive it.
stories.reflection: The birth is told almost entirely through what the world did not see: a sky clearing, winds turning gentle, rivers settling. The wonder is not announced to the city but to the elements, and it is all the more moving for being unheard.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana adds that when Vasudeva first looked upon the child he beheld a four-armed form holding the conch, discus and mace, and begged him to conceal it; that moment is told separately in this collection.
stories.next_story_tease: But the night was not over: the river still lay between the child and safety.
stories.hero_scene: A newborn Krishna in the dark of the prison cell while, unseen beyond the walls, the night turns calm: stars brighten, rivers settle, and flowers drift down from the sky.
visual_elements: flowers falling unseen from the sky
stories.variant_notes: VP 5.3 also includes the four-armed form and withholding of it (see 'reveal_form').

stories.title: Kamsa Comes to Slay the Newborn Girl
stories.story:
The message came in the night and tore Kamsa from his sleep. The palace at Mathura lay dark and still around him, and the knock had sounded like the thing he had spent years refusing to believe would come.

For years he had been waiting and dreading this news. The prophecy spoken at his sister's wedding had never left him: Devaki's eighth child would be his death. One by one he had destroyed the children born before this one, dashing them as they came into the world, so that no child could grow into the doom that had been promised to him. Every knock at his door in the dark hours had carried the same question, and now, at last, the answer had come. The guards came quickly to tell him what had happened, and he understood at once that the hour he feared had arrived. They told him a daughter had been born in the prison in the night.

He rose from his bed in an instant, wild-eyed and agitated, certain in his heart that this was the moment, and rushed to the prison. His feet carried him through the corridors faster than thought, and the guard at the cell door stepped aside for him.

In the cell, Devaki held her newborn close. She was the king's own younger sister, but she had spent her years of motherhood in a locked room, watching each child taken from her before she had truly had the chance to hold it. When she saw her brother in the doorway, she began to plead, and her voice was full of grief. She did not speak to him as a prisoner to a king, but as a sister to a brother. The lamplight fell soft on the child in her arms, and on her face, which was thin with the years of watching and loss.

“You have killed so many of my children already,” she said, “children who were bright as fire. I am your own younger sister, wretched, with my sons taken from me. Spare this one. She is only a girl. Have mercy.”

The words were simple, and they carried the whole of her grief. The children she had lost she remembered as bright as fire, a mother's way of saying they had been alive, and shining, and hers. She did not ask for freedom, or for justice, or even for her own life. She asked only that this one small child be allowed to live. Of all the things a mother can ask, it was the smallest and the largest at once.

But Kamsa did not hear her. Her words reached his ears, but they did not reach him; the prophecy stood between them like a wall of iron. Fear is older than mercy, and his fear was very old. He reached down and tore the child from her hands, and raised her up.

In the lamplight of the cell, the king held the child aloft, and the mother's plea hung in the air, unanswered. What he meant to do next, and what happened instead, belongs to the moment that follows.
stories.reflection: Devaki's plea names the cruelty plainly: she is not an enemy but his younger sister, and the children he has already taken were bright as fire. It is the plainness of her grief, not any violence shown, that makes the scene hard to read.
stories.content_note: Kamsa tears a newborn from its mother's arms and raises it to dash it; the child is not harmed within this story.
stories.next_story_tease: In the village of Gokul, an unexpected visitor was already drawing near.
stories.hero_scene: Kamsa in the lamplight of the prison cell, having torn the newborn girl from Devaki's arms and raised her up, while Devaki reaches toward him in grief.

stories.title: Vasudeva Carries Krishna Across the Yamuna
stories.story:
Vasudeva could not have said where the thought came from. It was not his own, this certainty; it arrived like a quiet command he had somehow been waiting to hear. The child was only a few hours old, and the prison was locked and guarded, and yet he knew, with a calm that surprised him, that he must carry the child out, now, in the middle of the night.

He lifted the baby from the lying-in room and stepped toward the door. The child lay quiet against his chest, and the cell behind them was dark and close. Outside, the guards slept where they stood. It was not ordinary sleep; it had come over them like a spell, the kind that takes a man in the middle of his watch and leaves him dreaming on his feet. It was as if the goddess of sleep herself had passed among them and drawn down their eyelids. Even the townspeople beyond the walls were asleep, and not a door creaked and not a dog stirred as he passed.

And the doors of the prison opened by themselves. As Vasudeva approached with the child, the great doors swung back on their own, the way darkness gives way before the sun. Bar and bolt gave no sound, and the iron that should have held him let him through as though it had been waiting for him all along.

Then he was outside, and the night was not kind. It was raining hard, a heavy rain falling from the clouds of night, pouring down as if the sky meant to test him. The rain came down in sheets, and the road toward the river turned to mud under his feet. But Vasudeva did not slow. He walked on through the storm with the child pressed to his chest. And as he walked, something followed him, not a guard, not a man, but Shesha, the many-headed serpent, who spread his hoods wide above the father and the child like a living roof, so that not a drop touched them. The rain beat on the serpent's hoods and ran off in streams to either side, and between them the father walked dry.

He came to the Yamuna, the great river, and it was in full flood, deep and swift and foaming, its waters dark and rising. In places its current dragged at the banks with the pull of whirlpools, and a man alone might have turned back. But the river knew what it carried. As Vasudeva stepped into the water, the Yamuna parted. It made a path for him, and the waters that would have been chest-deep were stilled and rose no higher than his knee. The water that should have swallowed him held itself back, as if bowing. He crossed with the child held close, and the river let them pass.

On the far bank he did not look back. He carried the child on through the storm toward Gokul, the settlement of the cowherds across the water, where the child would be kept safe. Behind him, the river closed over the path again, and the rain went on falling, and no one in the sleeping city knew that anything had happened at all.
stories.reflection: Every lock, watchman, and mile that should have stopped him instead opened, slept, or gave way. The escape is told not as a man overcoming obstacles but as a line of protection drawn around the child: a spell on the guards, a serpent for a roof, and a river that stands aside.
stories.next_story_tease: But Kamsa would not wait for morning.
stories.hero_scene: Vasudeva wading through the parted waters of the Yamuna at night, the newborn held against his chest, while the many-headed serpent Shesha spreads his hoods above them like an umbrella against the rain.

stories.title: Krishna Drains the Demoness Putana's Life
stories.story:
Gokul slept. The cowherd settlement lay dark, its doors shut, its cattle folded into their pens, and the night itself seemed to hold its breath. Through that darkness a woman moved from house to house, stopping at each doorway and looking in at the sleeping families, and no dog barked and no watchman stirred as she passed.

She was not a woman. She was Putana, a demoness known in many villages only as a name spoken in whispers — a child-killer who moved through the world the way sickness does, quietly, at night, drawn to the very young. She had come to Gokul to find a child, and she went from house to house, searching.

By chance, or by some darker purpose, her wandering brought her to the house of Nanda. There, in a dim room, an infant lay asleep — a child the whole settlement held dear. Putana lifted him from where he lay, cradled him against her, and gave him her breast.

There was milk in it, and there was something else as well. A poison lay there, meant for just such a child, laid to reach him through the very act that should have nourished him, and to still him as he fed.

The baby's eyes stayed closed, as if in sleep. He did not wake. He did not cry. He closed his mouth over her breast and began to drink, and it must have seemed to her, in that quiet room, the easiest thing she had ever done.

But what he drew from her was not milk alone. He drew out her life along with it, and she felt it going.

"Let go," she cried. "Let go of me."

The child did not let go. He drank on, and her cry rose out of that quiet house, terrible and deep. It rang across the settlement, and the earth shook with it, and the mountains, and the sky, and the very stars and planets in their slow paths trembled at the sound of it.

Then the life went out of her, and she fell.

As she fell, she was no longer the woman who had moved so quietly through the dark. She crashed down in her own form — monstrous, vast, her hair flung loose, her arms and legs thrown wide — and lay sprawled on the ground of Gokul like a great demon struck down out of the sky by a thunderbolt.

The child lay where he had been thrown, whole and unharmed. When the household woke and ran out, they found them there together: the baby they loved, and the dreadful thing that had come for him in the night.

They could make no sense of it. A demon had crept in to feed the child death, and the child had turned the feeding back upon her, and now she lay fallen in the yard while he lay beside her, whole and unharmed, as if the night's horror had never touched him at all. By daylight they carried the great body away, and the settlement slowly returned to its work; but the child fed and slept as on any other day, as if the whole night had been no more than a bad dream.

Long afterward, when the boy had grown and gone from the world, Uddhava would speak of Putana with a strange tenderness. The very demoness, he said, who had pressed her poisoned breast to the child with murder in her heart — even she had been received, by that same act, as a nurse, and granted a mother's place. What she had meant to do was not undone by this. But in the memory of it, it was not the last word either.
stories.reflection: Putana came to destroy the child, yet the tradition remembers her with tenderness: the very act of violence, offered to him, became her path to a mother's place. The story does not soften her cruelty, but it refuses to make cruelty the last word.
stories.content_note: A demoness attempts to poison an infant and dies; her death is described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: Putana was not the last danger to find the baby in Gokul.
stories.hero_scene: In a dark cowherd courtyard at night, an infant Krishna lies unharmed on the ground while beside him sprawls the monstrous, vast true form of the demoness Putana — hair flung loose, arms and legs thrown wide — her fall like a demon struck from the sky by a thunderbolt.

stories.title: Trinavarta Is Crushed by the Child's Weight
stories.story:
One afternoon the sky over Gokul turned strange.

It began as a wind — a dry, rising wind that lifted the dust of the lanes and set the doors to banging. The cattle stirred in their pens and lowed uneasily, and the women at their churning looked up and shaded their eyes. Then the wind thickened and darkened and began to spin, and those who looked up saw that it was not a storm at all. There was something inside it, and it was moving toward the house of Nanda.

It was Trinavarta, a demon who came as a whirlwind, and before anyone could cry out he swept down, snatched the baby from the courtyard where he lay, and carried him up into the spinning air.

The child vanished into the dust. The settlement was plunged into a choking darkness. Mothers groped for their own children and called their names, and no one could say where the boy had gone. High above, Trinavarta rose, clutching his prize, and the earth fell away beneath him.

But something was wrong.

The child in his arms was growing heavy. He had been nothing — a feather, a leaf — and now he pressed down on the demon like a stone. Trinavarta climbed, and the child grew heavier. He strained to rise higher into the sky, and the child grew heavier still, until the whirlwind demon found that he could not move at all. A child is the lightest thing in the world, and yet the sky could not hold this one; the demon who had risen like smoke now hung motionless, pinned by something he could not see or understand. It was as though he were holding up a mountain. As though he were holding up the whole weight of the world.

The wind, which a moment before had borne him aloft so easily, now held him fast; he could neither rise nor turn. His flight stopped. Then the baby's small hands closed around his throat, and Trinavarta could neither move nor breathe. His eyes started from his head.

And he fell.

He fell out of the sky onto a rock below, and the rock shattered him — the whirlwind broken to pieces on the stone. The cowherds ran to the place, expecting the worst, and found the child lying safe upon the demon's chest, as if the fall had been a cradle and the monster his bedding. The mothers who had lost sight of him in the dust came running too, and found him not only alive but unmarked, and they pressed him close and wept with relief. They passed him from hand to hand, turning him over to look for a wound, and found none.

They could not believe their eyes. A demon had carried the boy off to his death, and here he was, back among them, unhurt, as though the whole thing had been no more than a game of the wind. "What penance have we done?" they asked one another. "What worship, what good deeds, what kindness to other beings, that the child who was taken from us has been given back alive?"

They lifted him up and carried him home, and for a long time the men of Gokul would speak of the wonders they had seen in that broad forest. Nanda, the cowherd chief, kept his own counsel, but he had begun to notice how many wonders gathered around this quiet child — and how, one after another, they all ended the same way: with the boy safe, and the danger gone. He did not speak of it, but he began to watch the child more closely.
stories.reflection: The demon meant to carry the child off into the sky, and instead he was brought down by the very thing he tried to steal — a smallness that held the weight of the world. The rescue is not a struggle of equals; it is the unmasking of what the child already carried.
stories.content_note: A demon is crushed in a fall; the description is brief and not graphic.
stories.hero_scene: A demon in whirlwind form crashes out of a dark, dust-choked sky onto a rock, shattered, while the infant Krishna lies safe and unharmed upon his chest in the aftermath.
visual_elements: mood of sudden rescue and wonder

stories.title: Garga Secretly Names Rama and Krishna
stories.story:
Most ceremonies are made to be witnessed, but a naming can be a dangerous thing. When the family priest Garga came to Nanda's house in Gokula, he asked that the rites be done in secret.

Garga had not come on his own. He had been sent by Vasudeva, the man from whose arms the child had been carried to Gokula as a newborn, to perform the rites that every child must receive. The reason for the secrecy waited a few days' journey away, in Mathura. There a king named Kamsa was hunting for Vasudeva's children, and he would not have wanted a single one of them to live.

Nanda had not expected the old priest, and the sight of him at the door filled Nanda with joy. He rose at once and pressed his palms together. He washed Garga's feet and seated him with honor, and offered him the welcome due to a guest, and only then, with careful and pleasant words, did he make his request. It was no small thing to ask a priest to one's home, and Nanda asked it with the courtesy of a man asking a great favor. Of all those who know the things beyond the senses, he said, it is you who should perform these rites. For Garga could read the course of the stars as they moved through the sky, and he saw with a knowledge that did not come through the eyes.

Garga answered him plainly, and in a low voice. Kamsa, he said, is a man of evil mind, and he knows of your friendship with Vasudeva. If a naming in Gokula were spoken of, word would travel, and questions would follow, and the child would be in danger. Let this be done quietly, with no one to see and no one to tell.

So it was. There, in that room, without the knowledge of the other cowherds, Garga performed the rites. To the elder boy, the son of Rohini, he gave the name Rama — the boy who would also come to be called Balarama. And to Nanda's son he gave the name Krishna. The two names sat lightly on the two sleeping children, as if they had been waiting for them all along.

Then Garga spoke of what he could see, and his words fell soft in the quiet room. This child, he said, has not come into the world for the first time. In age after age he appears, and in each age his form takes a different color; he comes under many names, for the names and forms of this boy are beyond counting. And before this birth, Garga said, he was born of Vasudeva. The cowherds and all of Gokula would find their welfare in him. Through him the good would be shielded from those who did them harm, and the wicked would be kept at bay. He would be the delight of the cowherds and of all Gokula, Garga said, and the source of every good thing that came to them. Those who set their hearts on him, Garga said, are fortunate indeed. He is equal, Garga said at last, to Narayana himself in his qualities.

When the rites were done, Garga left as quietly as he had come, and Nanda spoke to no one of what had been said in that room. The two names were given in secret and held in secret.

And yet they did not stay secret. The name Krishna, first spoken behind a shut door in Gokula, would one day be spoken in every home and every temple, and on the lips of the whole world.
stories.reflection: Garga's secret naming holds the whole shape of Krishna's early life in miniature — the fear of Kamsa that forces concealment, and the quiet certainty that what is hidden now will not stay hidden.
stories.hero_scene: The sage Garga, seated in Nanda's dim home, performs the naming rites in secret, the two infants before him, as Nanda looks on with his palms pressed together.
visual_elements: a dim, closed room in Gokula

stories.title: Krishna Shows the Cosmos in His Mouth
stories.story:
One day Krishna was playing with his brother Rama and the other cowherd boys, tumbling in the dust of the lane the way small boys do, and when the game was done the boys came running to Yasoda with news.

"Krishna ate mud," they told her, all of them at once, their faces bright with the importance of the news. "We saw him. He ate dirt while no one was looking." They were certain of it; they had been playing with him all afternoon, and they knew what they had seen.

Now, whether he had eaten it or not, Yasoda was his mother, and a mother must ask. She took him by the hand and drew him to her, and scolded him, but gently, the way a mother scolds a child she is trying to keep safe — not so much angry as wanting the truth.

"Why did you eat mud," she asked, "in secret, when no one was looking? You know it is not good for you."

"I did not eat it, mother," Krishna said, meeting her eyes. "They are all saying what is not true."

Yasoda looked at him. There was a simple way to settle it, the oldest trick a mother knows.

"Then open your mouth," she said. "If you have eaten nothing, there will be nothing to see."

And Krishna opened his mouth.

What Yasoda saw there is beyond telling, and yet it has been told for thousands of years. In the small mouth of her small son she saw the whole universe. She saw the earth with its mountains and its oceans, and the sky, and all the directions, and the slow turning circle of the stars and planets. She saw water and fire and air and the vast space between them. She saw every living thing, and time itself, and the endless tangle of deeds and their results, and all the hidden differences between one being and another, moving together inside a child's open mouth — the whole world, moving and unmoving, held in the span of a few small teeth. She saw it all, and yet his mouth was small enough to kiss.

The same vision that the sages spend whole lifetimes seeking through the Vedas and the Upanishads and the long, patient disciplines of knowledge — she saw it in a single moment, freely given, in her son's open mouth.

She stood still, overwhelmed, and her own mind asked the only questions it could form. Is this a dream? she thought. Is it some divine illusion? Or is it a delusion that has come over my own mind?

And because she could not hold the vision, she reached for the ordinary truths that had always held her. I am Yasoda, she told herself. This is my husband Nanda. This is my son. I am the wife of the lord of Vraja, the mistress of all his wealth. And the child in front of her was only her child again.

Then the vision was veiled from her, as gently as it had come. Her memory of it slipped away, and she did not remember that she had ever seen the universe. She bent down, lifted her son onto her lap, and was simply his mother again, and the world, for that hour, was small and ordinary.

She would not remember. That, perhaps, was the mercy of it — that after seeing everything, after holding the whole of creation in a single glance, she was given back the one thing that mattered most, and it fit, again, in her two arms. And that, in the end, was enough.
stories.reflection: The story shows the infinite and then gently takes it back. Yasoda is not denied the vision because she is unworthy, but because her love needs him small; the mother who has seen the whole cosmos in his mouth is given back the child she can hold, and that is presented not as a loss but as a mercy.
stories.next_story_tease: And the days went back to being ordinary again — which, in that house, meant mischief.
stories.hero_scene: Yasoda kneels before the toddler Krishna, whose small open mouth reveals a vast, luminous universe within it — mountains, oceans, stars, and planets turning — while she stares, overwhelmed.

stories.title: Krishna Breaks the Butter Pot
stories.story:
Yasoda was churning. She sat at the churn, working the rope with both arms, and the whole of her told the story of a mother's long morning: the cloth bound at her waist with its cord, the garland of jasmine slipping from her hair, the sweat on her face, the small rings at her ears swinging as she pulled, her bangles shifting with every strain of the rope. It was the kind of morning that promised to be long and uneventful, and Yasoda was glad of it. The curd turned in the pot, and the butter was nearly ready.

Then her son came to her. He was hungry, and he came and stood close, pulling at her and wanting to be held, and she could feel the churn slow as she turned to him.

She lifted him onto her lap and nursed him, and as he fed she looked down at his face and smiled. It was the still, warm moment of the day.

It did not last. Behind her, the milk she had set to boil — forgotten in the warmth of that moment — climbed the sides of its pot and began to spill, hissing onto the coals. Yasoda had to set the child down and run to it. She left him there beside the churn.

He did not take well to being put down. One moment he had been warm and fed and held; the next, he was alone on the floor.

His lower lip began to tremble. He bit it with his small teeth, angry, and looked at the churn-pot — the pot full of fresh butter — and then he broke it. The pot fell apart, and all the butter of the morning's churning lay open before him.

He took up the butter, and, being a child left to his own devices, he did not eat it all himself; with no one there to tell him otherwise, he ate only what he pleased and shared the rest. He climbed up on the upturned mortar where it stood, and there, out of Yasoda's sight, he held out the butter, and a monkey — one of the creatures that wandered freely through the cowherd lanes — came and took it from his hand, and ate it with as much delight as if it had been a feast.

When Yasoda came back and saw the broken pot and the butter gone, she understood at once who had done it. She picked up a stick.

The boy saw the stick. He scrambled down and ran — as if he were afraid, though anyone watching would have seen that his fear was a game. And his mother ran after him.

It was a curious chase. The same child whose mind, the scriptures say, even the yogis in their long austerities cannot reach or enter — he was running through his own courtyard, and his mother was gaining on him. She ran with her full, swaying burden, her waist slender above it, her breath coming short, and still she could not quite catch him.

At last he let himself be caught. And when she had him, he did the thing that undid all her anger: he rubbed his eyes with his small, sooty hands — hands black with the collyrium and ash of the morning — and he cried, with tears that left black smears down his cheeks, the very picture of a wronged and sorry child. And Yasoda, who had come running with a stick, found the stick hanging loose in her hand, her anger already gone. The butter, the chase, the broken pot — none of it mattered now.
stories.reflection: The comedy is gentle because it turns on a real child's logic: interrupted at the breast, he takes the next sweet thing and shares it, then runs and pretends to cry. Even the line that the yogis cannot reach him lands lightly — the point is not his power but that a mother's chase is the one pursuit he never really outruns.
stories.next_story_tease: Yasoda's anger would not last, and soon she would go looking for a rope.
stories.hero_scene: In a sunlit cowherd courtyard, a young Yasoda chases a giggling toddler Krishna past an overturned churn and a broken butter pot, a stick raised in one hand and a half-eaten lump of butter in his.

stories.title: Krishna Uproots the Twin Arjuna Trees
stories.subtitle: How he came to be called Damodara
stories.story:
Krishna was still a crawling child, too young to walk, when the people of Gokula learned that he could not be kept still. He went into the cow sheds and came out gray with ash and dust. He rolled in the cow dung and only laughed. With his small body pasted in ashes and powdered cow-dung, he shone like a little prince of fire. He wandered into every corner of the village, and Nanda could not check him, and his mother Yashoda could not keep pace with him. When she caught him and began to scold him, he looked back at her with such innocent eyes that the scolding died on her lips, and she laughed in spite of herself.

One day, though, the mischief went too far, and Yashoda's patience ran out for good. Worked up with real anger, she took up a length of rope. She fastened it around the boy's waist and tied the other end to a heavy wooden mortar, the great block on which the household pounded its grain. Now go, she told him, go where you will — if you can. Then she turned back to her work, certain the matter was settled.

It was from that day, and from that rope, that he came to be called Damodara, the one bound by a rope around his belly. But a rope could not hold him. Dragging the mortar after him, Krishna left the courtyard and made his way toward the edge of the forest, where two great arjuna trees stood side by side — twin trees, tall and straight, grown huge with years, their branches laced together in the canopy. He went out meaning to surprise the people of Gokula and to play a game that only he understood. The mortar scraped behind him over the packed earth, heavier than he was, yet he dragged it as if it weighed nothing at all. At the edge of the forest the two trees rose up before him, straight as two pillars of an unseen gate.

He crawled between the trees, pulling the mortar through the narrow space. The mortar caught against their roots and held. Krishna pulled, and pulled again, harder. And with a single tug the two trees tore up out of the earth, roots and branches and all, and came crashing down with a sound that carried through the whole of Gokula. Birds burst from the fallen branches. Dust rose in a pale cloud and hung in the air, and for a long moment no one moved. The earth where the trees had stood lay torn open, and their long roots, thick as a man's arm, pointed up at the sky.

The cowherds came running at the noise, and they stopped short at what they saw. There stood no great trees now, only two fallen trunks, their great crowns thrown across the path. And Krishna, still tied to his mortar, only laughed, as if to show them all what a child could do.

But those two trees had not always been trees. They were two sons of Kubera, the lord of wealth, who had been cursed by a divine sage to stand rooted in the earth until someone set them free. Tall as they were and broad as their branches spread, they were prisoners, and no one in Gokula had ever guessed it. The sage's word had been waiting all those years to come true. Year after year the two had stood in their green stillness, leaf and branch instead of arms and legs. It was to make that word good that Krishna passed between them. A child too small to be trusted out of the yard had, with one pull, ended their long imprisonment and drawn the two of them back into the light.

When the dust settled, the two great trees lay still upon the ground. And between them sat a crawling child, a rope still at his waist, laughing.
stories.reflection: The story holds two wonders in one image: a child too small to walk brings down two great trees, and beneath their crash two cursed beings are set free. The binding meant to restrain him becomes the very thing that liberates.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana fold the earlier rope-binding into this episode; the Bhagavata opens with Krishna already bound — Damodara.
stories.hero_scene: A crawling child, a rope tied around his waist to a heavy wooden mortar, sits laughing between two great fallen arjuna trees, their roots torn from the earth.
stories.variant_notes: HV/VP fold in the mortar-binding beat.

stories.title: Krishna Kills Aghasura and Revives His Friends
stories.story:
Aghasura was a demon, and he had come to the forest in the shape of an immense python. The forest had gone quiet around him, as though the birds had understood before anyone else what lay stretched along the ground. The cowherd boys of Vrindavan, out with their calves, had gone into his open mouth, and now they lay inside him, alive but trapped, not yet swallowed. What had drawn them in, the account does not say; only that they had gone in, and not come out.

Krishna saw it, and the sight pierced him with pity. These were his friends, his own companions, and they were inside the belly of a demon, helpless, with no one in the world to turn to but him. He was amazed, too, at what fate had done. What use, he reasoned, was the life of this wretch? And how could the harm to these innocent ones be undone? Could both be accomplished at once, the death of the evil one and the saving of the good? He saw that it could, in a single stroke, and he did not hesitate. He walked into the demon's mouth.

The gods, watching from behind the clouds, cried out in fear. They had seen what a demon could do to a child, and they did not yet know that they were watching a god undo it.

Inside, Krishna grew. He grew until the demon's throat was blocked, until the great serpent could neither swallow nor breathe. He grew past its teeth and its throat, and the darkness inside it gave way before him. Its eyes bulged, and it writhed this way and that, and its vast body thrashed against the earth as the air was cut off from it. It had meant to hold the whole herd in its belly, and instead it found that it could not even draw a breath. And as its last breath left it, the boys and their calves, who had lain lifeless inside, Krishna raised up and led them out into the open air, alive again.

As the demon died, a great light rose from its body and stood blazing, filling all ten directions with its splendour, like a second moon or the sun coming up at night, and the light entered Krishna.

Then the sky broke into sound. The gods rained flowers down. The gandharvas sang and the apsaras danced, and the brahmins raised their hymns, and all of heaven celebrated the boys' return. And where the demon had fallen, only its dried skin remained, stretched across the ground of Vrindavan, a wonder that would not soon be forgotten. The boys looked at it for a long time before they gathered their calves and started for home.
stories.reflection: The story's emphasis falls not on the killing but on the great light that leaves the demon and enters Krishna, and on the boys walking out alive. Even for an enemy, the account holds out release rather than destruction.
stories.content_note: A demon in python form swallows the cowherd boys and calves; he is overcome without graphic detail.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna walking out of the open mouth of a vast python lying dead across the forest floor, leading the cowherd boys and their calves out behind him, as a great light rises into the sky.

stories.title: Krishna Becomes Every Calf and Boy
stories.story:
One day the calves and the cowherd boys of Vrindavan vanished, and no one could say where they had gone. The boys had walked out to the pasture that morning with their staffs and their flutes, driving the calves before them, and they simply did not come back. As the afternoon stretched toward evening the mothers stood in their doorways, listening. The cows shifted in their pens and lowed into the quiet for calves that did not answer. The whole village seemed to have lost its young at once.

Krishna had been with the boys, and he knew exactly where they had gone. He could have undone the thing in a moment, set every child and every calf back in its place with a word. But he chose a gentler way, one meant not merely to repair what was missing but to fill the waiting hearts of the mothers and the cows.

He became them. Standing at the edge of the pasture, Krishna expanded himself into every vanished calf and every vanished boy. Into each small body he entered, taking on not only the face and the limbs but everything that made that child that particular child — his staff and his horn, his flute and the leaf he carried, his ornaments and his clothes, and deeper than these, his temperament, his speech, his name, his age, the very way he walked and played. All of it, the old verses say, became full of the Lord.

Then each boy gathered his own calf and walked home to his own house. In the cow-pens the cows hurried forward, calling to their calves with a lowing that filled the evening air, and the calves ran to them as though they had never been away. In the houses the mothers rose at the first note of a flute, ran out, and lifted their sons into their arms. They held them close and would not put them down, kissing them, washing them, dressing them, marking their foreheads with tilak and setting food before them, asking nothing, needing no answer. The lost thing had come back, and that was all they required.

And the strange and tender thing was this: their love did not simply return. It grew. The cows loved their calves, and the women loved their sons, with a warmth greater than they had felt before — because what they held in their arms was not their own child but the Lord himself, playing the part of each one, and not a soul suspected it.

So it went, not for a day or a week, but for a full year. Morning after morning the boys who were Krishna drove the calves who were Krishna out to the pastures, and evening after evening they came home to mothers who, without knowing it, were loving God as their own. The affection in those homes climbed daily, the way a vine climbs, leaf by leaf, in a season no one counts. By the end of that year the mothers had been given something no one could have asked for: a whole year of loving, without knowing it, the very one for whom their love had always been meant.

It is a strange and beautiful picture. The mothers believed they were pouring their love into their own sons, and in one sense they were; in another, they were giving it straight into the hands of the one who had come into the world to receive it. Krishna did not set the world right by snapping his fingers. He set it right by becoming the thing those mothers loved, and letting their love find him where he stood, hidden in a hundred doorways, smiling up at a hundred faces that had no idea who they held.
stories.reflection: The episode turns on a quiet paradox: the mothers' love deepened precisely when its object was Krishna, though they did not know it. Love, the story suggests, is not made less real for being offered in ignorance — it is simply received by the one who was always its true object.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet a wildfire was soon to sweep through the forest toward the herd.
stories.hero_scene: In the doorway of a cowherd home a mother lifts her small son high and kisses his head, while in home after home across Vrindavan other mothers do the same with their own boys — every one of them Krishna, wearing a different child's face.

stories.title: Krishna Swallows the Wildfire and Saves the Herd
stories.story:
The fire came without warning, and it came from every side at once. One moment the cowherd boys were out in the Vrindavan woods with their cattle, the afternoon hot and still around them, the grass dry from a long stretch of sun; the next the grass was alight, and the flames were running toward them like a closing hand. They had spent the day as they always spent it, driving the herd from one pasture to the next, the calves at the cows' heels, and now the woods themselves had turned against them.

The boys had nowhere to turn. The smoke bent the trees and darkened the sky, the cattle lowed and bunched together in the middle of the clearing, and the boys, who were only children, saw the fire lean in toward them from all around. It was not the slow, watchful fire of a hearth. It moved with a roar, and the dry grass fed it as fast as it could burn. They called out to Krishna, who was among them, and their cry was simple: surely those who belong to you, Krishna, do not deserve to perish like this.

Krishna did not argue with them and did not run. He told them not to fear. Close your eyes, he said, and do not open them until I tell you. And they did. They did not ask him how, or why, or whether it would work; they simply shut their eyes, the way a child shuts them when a game requires it, except that this was no game. They stood in the middle of the burning forest, the roar of the fire all around them and the heat on their faces, and not one of them opened his eyes. It was trust, plain and simple, and it was all he asked of them.

What happened next none of them saw. Krishna drew the raging fire into his mouth and drank it down, the whole of it, flame by flame, until the heat and the roar and the smoke were gone. When at last he told them to open their eyes, they were not standing in the burning forest at all. They were at Bhandira, safe, and their cattle stood with them, and not one of them was hurt. There was no smell of smoke left in the air, only the lowing of the cattle, settling.

The boys looked at one another, and at the trees around them, and then at Krishna, and they could find no words for it. They had walked into a ring of fire and had come out of it, and it had cost them nothing but the closing of their eyes. The account says only this: it was his yoga, his power, accomplished by his own maya. It does not explain it further, and perhaps no explanation is wanted.

And then, as if nothing at all had happened, the afternoon went on. The herd was whole, the boys picked up their day where they had left it, and they were home before dark. When they tried, later, to tell the elders what had happened, the words would not come out straight, and the elders smiled and let it go.
stories.reflection: The wonder of the episode is that it is told almost without explanation. Krishna asks for nothing from the boys but the closing of their eyes, and the fire is gone before they open them; the story names the power behind it and then returns, without comment, to an ordinary afternoon.
stories.content_note: A forest fire briefly surrounds the cowherd boys and their cattle; no one is harmed.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, a boy among boys, standing calmly at the centre of a ring of wildfire while the cowherd boys around him stand with their eyes shut and the cattle huddle behind them.

stories.title: Krishna Dances on Kaliya's Heads
stories.story:
The serpent had him. In the waters of the Yamuna, the great snake Kaliya had coiled himself around Krishna and was squeezing, and on the bank the people of Gokula stood watching, helpless — the women and children most of all, for it was on their account that Krishna had gone down into the water. There was no one to pull him out, and no one strong enough to try. The village could only stand at the water's edge and grieve.

Then Krishna paused. He looked at the frightened faces on the bank, and he made up his mind. Following the path a human boy would follow, he waited a single moment — and then he rose up out of the serpent's coils, as easily as a man rises from a loose rope.

Kaliya was not finished. His body crushed and stung, he rose up in fury and spread his hundred heads, and he stood in the water hissing, his eyes fixed on Krishna like burning coals, licking the air with a forked tongue. There was poison in his glance, and fire, and the water around him grew bitter with his fury. He struck, and Krishna turned. The two of them moved around each other in the river the way a king of birds circles its prey, each watching for an opening that never came. The serpent had never met anyone who could match his turns, and it unsettled him; the boy was always a step ahead, always just out of reach. Around and around they went, and with every turn the serpent's strength ebbed a little, until his heads began to droop one by one.

And then Krishna did the thing no one expected. He climbed. He stepped up onto the serpent's broad, raised heads, and he began to dance.

The heads of Kaliya were jewelled, and the rubies on them turned Krishna's feet red as he moved. He danced as lightly as if the waters were solid ground beneath him. Wherever a hood refused to bow, Krishna pressed it down with the sole of his foot, as a man presses down what will not yield. It was a hundred-headed thing, that serpent, but each head that rose in defiance was trampled back down, and the water around them began to darken, and Kaliya's body began to break, his strength bleeding out of him with every step of the dance.

From the sky the celestials watched, and they did not stay silent. The gandharvas and the siddhas and the sages and the wives of the gods came with drums and song and sweet music, and they showered flowers down upon the boy dancing on a serpent's heads, and they raised their voices in praise, as if it were the most natural stage in the world. To them the dance was not cruelty; it was a wonder, and they could not look away.

Kaliya's pride was being crushed one hood at a time. And then, as the dance went on and his strength left him, something turned in the serpent. He remembered the ancient being who holds within himself all that moves and all that stands still — Narayana — and in his mind, beaten and bleeding, he took refuge there.

It was then that the serpent's wives came forward through the water, their clothes and hair in disarray, their ornaments slipping, their faces full of grief, to stand before the boy who danced on their husband's heads.

And the dance slowed, and stopped. The river grew still again around them, and the only sound left was the breathing of a hundred tired heads.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not flee when the serpent's coils loosen; he climbs and dances. The discipline is precise rather than cruel — each hood that will not bow is pressed down, and it is this that finally turns the serpent's thoughts to refuge.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana fold this dance into the episode of Kaliya's banishment rather than treating it as a separate moment.
stories.content_note: Depicts Krishna overpowering the serpent Kaliya; the serpent is trampled and injured.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna dances on the raised, jewelled heads of the serpent Kaliya in the waters of the Yamuna, trampling each hood that will not bow, as the snake's many heads rear and hiss around him.

stories.title: Krishna Lifts Govardhana Hill
stories.story:
The rain began out of season, and it did not fall like rain. It fell in sheets and struck like stones. Hail rattled on the roofs, a wind rose that bent the trees flat, and in the pastures of Vrindavan the cattle trembled, pressing their calves against their sides. In the doorways the cowherds stood watching the sky turn black, and they cried out the one name they could think of: "Krishna! Krishna!"

Krishna understood at once what was happening. This was no ordinary storm. This was Indra, king of the gods and lord of the rain, and he was angry.

The anger had a reason. The cowherds had always kept a sacrifice to Indra, the worship of the god who sends the rains. But that year, at Krishna's urging, the cowherd king had offered a different sacrifice instead — a sacrifice of the cows — and the offering that had always gone to Indra was not made. Indra's pride was wounded, and a wounded god of rain knows one way to answer.

So the storm came, out of season, and the hail fell like stones, and the cowherds and their cattle stood in the open with nowhere to go.

Krishna looked at the people of Vrindavan, beaten by wind and falling ice, and he made his choice. This storm, he reasoned, had been sent by Indra in his anger, to make a show of his power over those who had turned away from his worship. And he resolved to answer it — not with anger of his own, but by sheltering his people, and by breaking the pride of those who fancy themselves lords of the world.

He called to the cowherds: come, all of you, with your cattle. Then, before their eyes, Krishna put out one hand — one hand — and lifted the whole of Govardhana hill. He raised it from the earth and held it aloft as lightly as a child holds up an umbrella, as lightly, they say, as if it sat on the tip of his finger.

"Under here," he said. "All of you. Bring the cows."

They did not need to be told twice. The cowherds and their wives, the children and the calves, the whole of Vrindavan crowded in beneath the hill. And there, under that one raised hand, they were dry.

For seven days and seven nights the storm went on. The clouds Indra had sent poured their rain upon the village, the hail fell, and the wind howled around the rim of the hill. But beneath Govardhana, held up by a child's hand, the people stood safe, and the cattle stood safe, and the storm could not reach them. It battered the hill from every side, and still the mountain did not waver, and still the hand beneath it did not tire.

Through all of it Krishna stood unmoved, the hill balanced on his hand, no more troubled by the weight of it than by the weight of a flower. The cowherds looked up at the mountain hanging above them, and down at the boy holding it, and for seven days they did not grow tired of looking.

On the seventh day the storm broke. The clouds emptied themselves and drifted away, the wind fell, and the rain stopped. Indra's pride was broken. He had sent the fury of the sky against Vrindavan, and it had done nothing. The people he meant to humble had stood dry beneath a hill held up by a boy.

Then Krishna set the hill down again. The people came out from under it into the washed, quiet air, and they looked at the child who had sheltered them, and they understood something they had not understood before.
stories.reflection: Krishna's answer to Indra's fury is not a counter-attack but shelter. The storm that was meant to humble Vrindavan instead reveals whose protection is real, and Indra's pride breaks not against force but against a hill held up for love of his people.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana specify that the rain lasted seven days and nights.
stories.hero_scene: A young Krishna holds Govardhana hill aloft on the raised palm of one hand like an umbrella, while cowherds, women, children and cattle crowd beneath it, safe and dry, as hail and rain lash the dark landscape beyond the hill's rim.

stories.title: The Gopis Abandon Their Homes
stories.story:
The moon came up full over Vrindavan, and it washed the eastern sky with a red that was almost the colour of fresh kumkum. The forest stood soft in that light, and the whole of it seemed to wait. The river below carried the light in broken pieces, and the air smelled of the year turning. It was one of those autumn nights when the heat of the day has gone and the earth gives back its warmth. Krishna looked at the night and at the forest, and he raised his flute and began to play.

The song did not call out to anyone by name. It was simply the flute on an autumn night, low and sweet, and it did not ask; it drew. It did not soothe; it quickened, the way a single note can set a whole evening leaning. It was the kind of song that makes a listener restless in her own house. It was the sound they had been waiting for without knowing it. It crossed the fields and the lanes and the courtyards of the village, and it made the quiet of the evening feel like a promise. The women of Vraja heard it, and their minds went out of them.

One of them was milking, and she left the cow standing with the pail half full and did not look back. One was serving the evening meal, and she set the dish down while it was still warm and walked out. One had a child at her breast, and she put the child down and went. One was anointing herself for the evening, and she stopped where she sat. One had kohl half applied to her eyes, and she left it there, one eye dark and the other bare. Each of them was in the middle of something, and each of them left it unfinished. The evening tasks lay where they had dropped, and the houses stood half-done, as though time had stopped inside them.

Husbands caught at their arms, and fathers and brothers called after them, and the hands of their kinsfolk closed over their wrists. It made no difference. Their voices rose and fell behind them, and were lost under the sound of the flute, which went on and did not hurry. They went, heedless of every restraint, because the sound of the flute had taken them and would not let them go.

Some of them could not go at all. The door was watched, or the house had closed in around them, and no way out could be found. Those women shut their eyes where they stood, some of them before they had even reached the door. The ache of being apart from the one they loved had grown unbearable and fierce, and in the shutting of their eyes it burned itself out, and whatever else had been in them went with it. With their eyes shut they went to him, and they found him as surely as the women who had crossed the fields.

By the time they reached him, the moon stood high over the Yamuna. Krishna saw the women of Vraja come near to him, the milkmaid with the pail half full, the one with kohl on a single eye, and those who had never left their courtyards at all but had come to him with their eyes closed. The night, which had begun so quietly, had gathered them all to one place on the riverbank, and behind them the village went on sleeping, unaware of who had slipped away from it. The Yamuna was there to meet them, dark and slow under the moon.
stories.reflection: What stays in the mind is the inventory of unfinished things, the milk half-milked and the eye half-painted. The gopis are not shown renouncing anything with ceremony; they simply drop what they are doing mid-task because the flute interrupted a normal evening and they answered it. The detail that some could not leave at all, and still reached him by closing their eyes, quietly widens the story: the going is outward, but the meeting is not limited by walls.
stories.next_story_tease: But the night was far from over; the dance had not yet begun.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna standing in moonlight playing his flute by the Yamuna, while gopis hurry toward him across dark fields, one still carrying a half-filled milk pail, another with kohl on only one eye.

stories.title: The Great Rasa Dance
stories.story:
The moon that rose over the Yamuna that autumn night was full and whole, and the forest lay silver beneath it. The river moved quietly, and the air was mild, and the whole of Vrindavan seemed to have settled into the kind of night that asks nothing of anyone. It was the season of clear nights, when the year turns and the moon hangs low and white. Krishna looked at the night and found it good for dancing. So it was that, on the bank of the river, he began the rasa dance, and the gopis of Vraja gathered around him.

He did not dance alone at the centre of the circle. He became as many as the women themselves, so that between every two gopis there stood a Krishna, and each one felt him near and no other beside her. In him they had found the one they loved beyond all others, and for those hours nothing else existed. The circle was bright with sound before it was bright with anything else, bangles and anklets and little bells keeping time in the dark.

They danced with the whole of themselves. Their feet found the beat and kept it; their arms swept and lifted; they bent at the waist, and their garments swayed, and their earrings swung against their cheeks. Their faces glistened with the effort, and their throats flushed as they sang aloud, and their hair came loose, and the flowers slipped from it without anyone stopping to notice. They sang of him as they danced, their voices rising above the water, and their songs, as much as their steps, belonged to the season, full of the clear night and the turning year. One of them sang with him in a single blended voice, as though the same note came from two throats. Another, weary from the dance, leaned on his shoulder for a moment and did not fall. One, as she moved, kept only the tinkling of her anklets and her girdle for company, and still she sang. In the ring they shone, it is said, like lightning moving within a circle of clouds.

High above, the women of the sky leaned out to watch, and the sight bewildered them: a ring of mortal women on a riverbank, and at every turn a god beside each of them. The gods rained flowers down on the dance. Petals fell on the water, on the grass, on the dark heads of the gopis as they circled, and the night filled with their fragrance.

As the night wore on, the gopis grew tired, and some of them, in the middle of their joy, put on a small show of pride, yet still they sang of his deeds, delighting in the touch of his hands. Where a face was hot from the dance, his hand was there, and the weariness of them seemed to matter to him more than the dance itself. He led them to the river to wash the heat of the dancing away. They went with him the way a herd follows its lord, and in the water they splashed him, laughing, and he let them. From the bright chariots above, more flowers came down, and with them the praise of those who watched, and Krishna, rejoicing in his own nature, took his ease among them.

In this way the moonlit nights of autumn passed, one after another, and Krishna, who wanted for nothing, kept the company of the women of Vraja under the moon, and the women kept his. The dance ended as it had begun, not with a word but with the moon high over the water.
stories.reflection: The multiplication is striking not as a display of power but as a form of attention: Krishna becomes many so that no gopi in the circle is left without him. What the sources linger on is not the miracle itself but the moonlight, the music, and the nearness.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna at the centre of a ring of gopis under a full autumn moon on the Yamuna bank, one form of him beside each woman, while flower petals drift down from the sky.
stories.variant_notes: bpc1_037 is Uddhava's recollection.

stories.title: Akrura Beholds the Divine Vision in the Yamuna
stories.story:
Akrura had been sent to Vrindavan to bring Krishna and Balarama to Mathura, where Kamsa reigned and their own parents waited, worn down by the king's cruelty. He had told the brothers plainly what lay ahead of them, and neither had flinched. Now, with the two of them riding in his chariot, he came to the banks of the Yamuna. The sun stood high and the river ran slow and clear, its water bright as a gem. He stopped the chariot and stepped down to wash, as a traveler does, and the two brothers waited on the road above.

Akrura stood at the water's edge and sipped a little, then waded in. Murmuring the eternal prayer, he sank beneath the surface — and what he saw unseated him. There in the river, as though no water separated them at all, sat the two sons of Vasudeva, still in the chariot, exactly as he had left them on the bank. He broke the surface for air, asking himself how the boys could be both on the road and in the river at once, and he dove again.

This time the river opened into something far larger than a riverbed. Before him rose the lord of serpents, Ananta, a being of a thousand heads crowned with a thousand spreading hoods, receiving the praise of all who gathered around him. And resting at ease in the coils of that great serpent was a figure dark as a rain-cloud, clothed in yellow silk, his face serene and lit with the faintest smile, his glance gentle and full of love. In his hands he held a lotus, a conch, a discus and a mace, and his long arms were bright with crown and bracelets and armlets. About him stood his attendants — Sunanda and Nanda, and the sages Sanaka and his brothers — and the great devotees of old, Prahlada and Narada among them. Around them shone the goddesses of fortune and nourishment, of speech and beauty and fame, of contentment and strength and glory, all gathered in attendance on the one who lay upon the serpent.

Akrura understood then what he was being shown. The two boys waiting patiently on the riverbank were not two boys. They were the Lord himself, resting upon Shesha, and the whole court of heaven attended him. He rose from the water trembling with joy, his devotion overflowing, and when he opened his mouth to speak the words came out broken and thick with feeling. He did not ask how this could be, or whether his eyes had deceived him; he simply praised, the name and the form he had just seen poured out in words that stumbled over one another, for what else can a man do who has looked into a river and found the source of everything looking back at him.

What makes the vision remarkable is its ordinariness before and after. A man stops his chariot, washes in a river, sees God face to face, and then returns to the road with two boys who are, and are not, the being he just beheld. He had set out that morning to escort two boys to a city, and he would arrive carrying in his memory the face of God. The river kept flowing and the sun kept its place, and no one on either bank knew what had happened in between. The words he had offered did not need to be elegant; they only needed to be true. Akrura climbed back onto the chariot and drove on toward Mathura, keeping the secret of the Yamuna close, and neither of his passengers said a word about it.
stories.reflection: Akrura's vision is given not to a sage in a forest but to a dutiful man washing in a river on a journey, at the most ordinary moment of his day. The story seems to insist that the divine is not hidden in some distant place but waits beneath the surface of what a person is already doing.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana describe Balarama himself as the thousand-hooded serpent with Vishnu resting upon him, while the Bhagavata here presents the serpent Ananta bearing the dark Lord, with both brothers present in the vision. This telling follows the Bhagavata.
stories.next_story_tease: Across the river, Mathura — and Kamsa — awaited them.
stories.hero_scene: Beneath the surface of the Yamuna, Akrura with folded hands gazes up at the thousand-hooded serpent Ananta, and resting in its coils the dark-complexioned Lord in yellow silk, holding a lotus, conch, discus and mace while gods and goddesses gather around him.
