stories.title: Arjuna's Despair and Collapse
stories.story:
The two armies had drawn up on the plain of Kurukshetra, and the war everyone had dreaded and prepared for was about to begin. Years of grievance and humiliation had been folded into this single hour. Every man on that field was someone's father, son, or brother; almost all of them shared the same blood. Then, before a single arrow flew, the man at its center lost the will to fight.

The Kauravas and the Pandavas stood facing each other, and the sound of their conches and drums and cymbals and horns filled the field. Duryodhana had walked the length of his own army naming its warriors to his preceptor Drona — Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Aswatthaman — and the venerable old grandsire Bhishma had raised his conch and blown a lion's roar. On the other side, standing on a great chariot yoked to white steeds, Krishna blew the conch Panchajanya and Arjuna blew Devadatta. The terrible Bhima blew his great conch Paundra, Yudhishthira blew Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughosa and Manipushpaka. The answering horns went up, and for a moment the whole plain was one vast, brazen noise.

And then Arjuna looked across the field, and everything stopped.

He saw the men arrayed before him, his own kinsmen on both sides. There was his grandsire Bhishma, the venerable old warrior who had presided over his whole life. There was his preceptor Drona, who had taught him the bow. There was Karna and Kripa and Aswatthaman, and beyond them cousins and kinsmen he had grown up beside, uncles and nephews and the sons of old friends. And behind him, in his own ranks, stood Subhadra's son, his own boy, and the sons of Draupadi. These were the men the war had gathered — and the men he was about to kill.

The pity came on him all at once, and it was not a small thing. His body began to tremble, and the hair stood on end along his skin, and his skin burned. It was not fear that did this; it was something nearer to love, and it was stronger than either. The great bow Gandiva, which had never failed him, slipped from his fingers — and with it slipped everything he had prepared for this day. He could not hold it. A man who cannot raise his bow cannot fight a war, and this man had been the hope of an entire side of it.

He spoke, despondent, to Krishna beside him. His voice, which had carried across a hundred battlefields, was low. 'I wish not to slay these though they slay me,' he said. 'O slayer of Madhu.' What kind of victory, he was asking without quite asking, would be bought with the deaths of his own people?

He did not wait for an answer, or perhaps he could not. His mind troubled with grief, he cast aside his bow and his arrows and sat down in the chariot, right there on the field of battle, between two armies that were waiting for him. The conches that had roared a moment before were silent; the field held its breath. The noise of the day fell away, and the man who was supposed to lead them all sat slumped and still.

Krishna did not speak yet. He held the reins, and he waited. There would be time for words soon, and the words would change everything. But for now there was only this: the strongest man on the field, undone not by any enemy but by the sight of the people he loved standing where he would have to kill them.
stories.reflection: The Gita does not begin with philosophy; it begins with a man falling apart. Before Krishna can teach Arjuna anything, Arjuna has to be honest about what he feels — and what he feels is that the victory he has spent his life preparing for is not worth the faces in front of him.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna had not yet spoken — and what he was about to say would become the heart of the teaching.
stories.hero_scene: Arjuna slumped in his chariot on the field of Kurukshetra, the great bow Gandiva slipped from his hand and his arrows cast aside, while Krishna stands quietly at the reins against the hush of two waiting armies.

stories.title: Krishna Reveals the Vishvarupa
stories.story:
The armies of the Kauravas and the Pandavas stood drawn up on the plain of Kurukshetra, waiting, and in the long pause before the first blow Krishna had been teaching. The despair that had brought Arjuna to his knees at the sight of his own kinsmen drawn up against him was gone. What Krishna had called the supreme mystery — the knowledge of the Self, spoken for his welfare — had dispelled his delusion. But in its place stood a hunger no teaching had yet satisfied. He had heard, at length, of how all beings come into being and pass away again, and of a greatness in Krishna that never diminished. He believed it. Believing was no longer enough. He had been taught the whole of it, and the teaching had left him with one thing still unfulfilled: he wanted to see, with his own eyes, the being who had been speaking to him.

"What you have said of yourself is true," Arjuna said at last. It was not a demand; it was trust. "I desire to behold your sovereign form. If you think that I am able to bear it, show me your eternal Self."

Krishna looked at him with eyes like lotus petals, and did not refuse. "Behold my forms by hundreds and thousands," he said, "divine, of many hues and many shapes. Behold the Adityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Aswins, the Maruts. Behold innumerable marvels never seen before. Behold, you of the curly hair, the entire universe — everything that moves and everything that does not — gathered together in this body of mine, and whatever else you may wish to see. But you cannot see me with these eyes of yours. I give you celestial sight. Behold my sovereign, mystic nature."

And then he showed him.

The form that rose before Arjuna had many mouths and many eyes, many wondrous aspects, celestial ornaments and weapons uplifted, garlands and robes of heaven, anointed with a fragrance that belonged to no earth. It was full of every wonder, resplendent, without end, its faces turned in every direction at once. Arjuna had known light his whole life — the sun, the fire, the lamps of evening — but nothing he had ever seen came near this. If the light of a thousand suns were to burst forth together in the sky, it would only resemble the light of that Mighty One.

In that single body Arjuna saw the entire universe, divided and subdivided into its many parts, all collected together. His hair stood on end, and he bowed his head and joined his hands, filled with amazement. When he spoke again his voice had changed. "I see all the gods," he said, "and all the varied hosts of creatures, and Brahman seated upon his lotus, and the rishis and the celestial serpents. I see you with arms and stomachs and mouths and eyes beyond counting, on every side, O you of infinite forms. Neither end nor middle nor beginning can I find in you, Lord of the universe, Lord of the universal form."

Still the vision pressed on him, and he looked and looked, unable to turn away. "Bearing your diadem, your mace and your discus," he said, "a mass of energy glowing on every side, I behold you — hard to look upon, blazing like fire at its full height."

There, between two armies that had not yet begun to fight, the man who held the reins of Arjuna's chariot stood revealed as the ground of everything. And the warrior who had asked to see it could only bow before what he had been shown.
stories.reflection: The vision is granted because Arjuna asks for it, and it overwhelms him not with threat but with scale: the whole of creation gathered into one form that has no end, middle, or beginning. What silences him is not fear of the form's power but the sight of every thing he has ever known held, at once, in a single body.
stories.next_story_tease: But the war would not wait long on vision; harder counsel lay ahead on that same field.

stories.title: The Ashvatthama Stratagem
stories.story:
Drona was cutting through the Pandava army, and nothing could stand before him. The Panchalas and the Srinjayas rushed at him in waves, yelling loud and fierce as they came, and his shafts and darts struck them down as fast as they arrived. They were mighty car-warriors, full of might and energy, and though he slaughtered them they were not yet afraid of him; still they came on, and still they fell. The carnage of steeds and men went on like the slaughter of the gods' enemies in some older age, and the sons of Kunti, afflicted with his shafts, felt fear enter their hearts and hope drain out of them. Drona alone seemed enough to undo them all. The day was theirs to lose, and Drona was taking it from them hour by hour.

"He will consume us all," they said to one another, "like a raging fire eating a heap of straw in the season of spring. There is no one who can even look at him in battle. And Arjuna — the one man who is a match for him — will not fight him." For Drona, conversant with the mightiest of weapons, had been Arjuna's own teacher, and Arjuna, who knew the ways of morality, would not raise his bow against the man who had taught him the bow.

It was Krishna who answered their despair — Krishna, endued with great intelligence and devoted to their welfare. "This foremost of all bowmen cannot be vanquished by force," he said, "not even by the gods with Indra at their head. But when he lays aside his weapons, he can be slain even by men. Cast aside virtue, sons of Pandu, and find some contrivance, before Drona of the golden car destroys us all. When his son Ashvatthaman has fallen, he will cease to fight. Let some man tell him that Ashvatthaman has been slain."

It was not the kind of counsel the brothers had expected from him, and it landed among them like a stone thrown into still water. Arjuna would not approve it; he heard the plan and rejected it. Others approved it. And Yudhishthira — the eldest, the one whose word was truth itself — accepted it only with the greatest difficulty. To save his brothers, he would have to become, for a little while, the instrument of a falsehood, and he agreed to carry it. It was the hardest thing he had yet agreed to in the whole war, and he accepted it with his head bowed.

So it was done, in a way that cut the truth down the middle. Bhima, the mighty-armed, took up his mace and slew a huge, terrible, foe-crushing elephant named Ashvatthaman, one that belonged to their own army, to Indravarman, the chief of the Malavas — their own war-elephant, struck down by their own mace, not to win any fight but to make a single sentence true. Then he approached Drona in the midst of the battle, and with some bashfulness cried aloud, "Ashvatthaman has been slain."

The words were true of the elephant that lay dead behind them. They were spoken to a father who would hear them as his son. There is a difference between a lie and a truth told to deceive, and the whole weight of that difference sat in Bhima's voice. Drona had heard a thousand war-cries that day and never once turned from his work, but this one name, spoken low, would do what no weapon on the field could. On the width of a name shared between a man and a beast, the whole battle was about to turn.
stories.reflection: The man who taught Arjuna the way of dharma on this same field now counsels him to lay that virtue aside, and the text refuses to smooth it over: Arjuna rejects the plan, Yudhishthira accepts it only with great difficulty, and the lie is built out of something technically true. The episode leaves the reader standing in exactly that discomfort, without a verdict.
stories.content_note: Battle violence and a wartime deception.
stories.next_story_tease: The battle did not end with Drona; ahead waited Karna, and an arrow meant for Arjuna alone.
stories.hero_scene: In the dust and noise of the battlefield, Bhima lowers his mace beside the fallen elephant named Ashvatthaman while, at a distance, the chariot of the aged Drona waits as the words of his son's death are carried toward him.
visual_elements: the weight of a shared name

stories.title: Krishna Sinks the Chariot
stories.story:
The duel Karna and Arjuna had been waiting for all their lives came at last, and for a long time no one could say who was winning. Everything hung on this duel, and both armies knew it. Arjuna's weapon had been swelling with energy and careering through the sky like lightning, consuming the Kauravas, and the broken divisions of their army had drawn back to a distance to watch it — until Karna crushed it with shafts winged with gold, using the great foe-killing weapon he had obtained from Rama, and turned it back. Then he bent his own loud-sounding bow, whose string could not be broken, and sent showers of shafts that pierced Arjuna again and again.

So the two of them closed with each other, and the sky went dark. They struck like two fierce elephants locking tusks. The points of the compass vanished behind their weapons, and the sun itself disappeared beneath the downpour of arrows, until the whole welkin was one vast web of shafts with no space between. The men watching from both armies could see nothing but arrows, and no one on either side could tell where the next one would come from. Two warriors, both accomplished in the use of weapons, wove every kind of beautiful manoeuvre, each of them watching for the other's single lapse — the one opening that would end it.

Now the son of the charioteer would press his rival back, now the diademed Arjuna would drive him in turn. The beings gathered in the sky shouted first "Excellent, O Karna!" and then "Excellent, O Arjuna!" while the earth was pressed deep beneath the weight of the cars and the trampling of steeds and elephants. It was a passage of arms so dreadful that the other warriors on the field could only stand and wonder.

And in that darkness of arrows, something else was waiting for its opening too. The snake Aswasena had long been hostile to Arjuna, and he had been sheltering in the arrow-net above the field, biding his time. Now he let himself be fitted to a shaft, and Karna, bending his loud-sounding bow, loosed him at Arjuna's head.

The shaft blazed as it flew through the welkin, alive and burning, aimed to end the duel at a stroke.

Krishna saw it coming — the way a man who has driven a thousand chariots sees the one arrow among ten thousand that matters.

With great speed and the greatest ease, he pressed down the chariot with his feet. The excellent car sank about a cubit into the earth, and the white steeds, white as the rays of the moon, bent their knees and laid themselves down on the ground.

The burning arrow passed low over Arjuna's head, close enough to graze it — and swept away only his diadem.

The crown fell to the earth, and the man who had worn it was still standing. The diadem was the mark by which the whole field knew Arjuna, and Karna's deadliest shaft had torn it from his head and left the head itself untouched. It had met a charioteer who would sink the very ground beneath his friend to keep that head upon his shoulders. In the middle of the greatest battle the world had ever seen, the moment that saved Arjuna came down to a man setting his feet a cubit deeper into the earth. The chariot rose again, the moon-white horses came back to their feet, and the duel went on — but the opening had passed, and it had passed because of the man holding the reins. Krishna had raised no weapon that day. He had not needed one.
stories.reflection: The episode makes Krishna's loyalty literal: he is not fighting, not speaking, only driving, and yet the whole outcome turns on his feet pressing a chariot into the earth. The divine protection here is not a weapon or a miracle of light but a quick, precise act of a charioteer who will not let his friend be taken.
stories.content_note: Battle violence; an arrow narrowly misses Arjuna.
stories.next_story_tease: But the duel between Karna and Arjuna was not yet decided.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, reins in hand, presses the chariot down into the earth with his feet as the white horses kneel, while Karna's blazing snake-arrow sweeps just over Arjuna's bowed head and knocks the diadem from his hair.

stories.title: Krishna Urges Arjuna to Slay the Distressed Karna
stories.story:
It was the war at Kurukshetra, and all through that long afternoon the sky had been turning into a net of arrows. Arjuna and Karna, the son of the charioteer Adhiratha, had been searching for each other's one lapse, and neither had yet given it. The two hosts had fallen back to watch, for it seemed the whole long war had narrowed at last to these two men alone, each of whom was desirous of availing himself of the other's lapses.

Arjuna had loosed a weapon that swelled with energy and went careering through the air with the effulgence of lightning, consuming the Kuru ranks, and the broken divisions of the Kauravas fled and stood at a distance, gazing at it. Karna alone held his ground. With showers of shafts winged with gold he baffled that burning weapon while it was still in the sky, and with a foe-killing weapon of his own, the great weapon he had obtained from Rama and which resembled in its efficacy an Atharvan rite, he crushed it and pierced Arjuna with keen shafts. Bending his own loud-sounding bow of unbreakable string, he shot showers of arrows, and the two of them closed.

They struck at each other like two fierce elephants striking with their tusks. The points of the compass became shrouded with weapons and the very sun went invisible. The sky turned into one vast arrowy net with no space between, and all the Kauravas and the Somakas beheld that wide-spread arrowy net, and in that dense darkness caused by arrows the two armies could make out nothing else. Those two foremost of men, both accomplished in weapons, kept aiming and shooting, and displayed diverse kinds of beautiful manoeuvres. Sometimes the Suta's son prevailed over his rival, sometimes the diadem-decked Arjuna prevailed, in prowess and weapons and lightness of hands, and every warrior on the field was filled with wonder. Even the beings in the welkin applauded, crying sometimes, Excellent, O Karna, and sometimes, Excellent, O Arjuna. And a serpent named Aswasena, who nursed an old hatred of Arjuna, had slipped into that arrowy darkness and was waiting there for his moment.

Then the turn came. The earth had been pressed deep all day with the weight of cars and the tread of steeds and elephants, and now it seemed to turn against one of its own. Karna's chariot wheel sank into the earth, and the ground held it, as though it had at last chosen its side. Karna stood stupefied. The man who had never shown his back in battle was held motionless in the open, in the sight of both hosts, and he could not draw his car free.

He called out to Arjuna and appealed to his righteousness. He was in distress, he said; he had been brought low not by his enemy's hand but by the ground itself. He did not ask for mercy, only for time, the chance to free his wheel and face Arjuna as an equal, as the dharma of warriors required. Let Arjuna remember dharma, he urged. Grant him one moment's respite, the bare moment that a warrior in his place could rightly claim.

Krishna, the younger brother of Indra, did not let the moment pass. Why, O son of Pandu, dost thou become so forgetful? he addressed him, with great excitement. They that are truly wise never spare their foes, however weak, even for a moment. Slay him, therefore, like Indra slaying the Asura Namuci.

Arjuna's arrow answered, and the warrior who had asked for a moment received none. The wheel stayed where the earth held it, and the duel was over.
stories.reflection: The two pleas stand side by side and the account does not step in to say which was right. Karna asks for what dharma owes a man brought low; Krishna answers that a war is no place for such debts, and names Indra and Namuci as the precedent. That the episode ends without resolving the argument is, perhaps, the point: the hardest questions are the ones the source leaves open.
stories.content_note: A warrior is slain in battle; the death is described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: But the war's grief was not finished; a mother's curse was about to fall upon Krishna.
stories.hero_scene: Karna standing motionless beside his chariot, its wheel sunk into the earth, calling out to Arjuna while Krishna urges Arjuna to strike, the sky above them dark with a net of arrows.

stories.title: Gandhari Curses Krishna; He Accepts with a Smile
stories.story:
The war was over, and the field at Kurukshetra lay strewn with the dead, and Gandhari walked among them and saw what a mother sees when the war is over. Her own sons lay dead among the rest, and with them it seemed she had lost everyone's sons, and she poured it all out to Krishna, who stood beside her.

Behold, she said, the ruler of the Kambojas, that bull-necked hero, lying in the dust though he deserved to rest at ease on soft Kamboja blankets. His wife is weeping bitterly at the sight of his blood-stained arms, those arms that once were smeared with sandal-paste; even now, adorned with beautiful palms and graceful fingers, they resemble a couple of spiked maces, and within their clasp joy never left her for a moment. What will be my end, the beauteous one cries, O ruler of men, when I am deprived of thee? Endued with a melodious voice, the Kamboja queen weeps helplessly and quivers with emotion.

Behold the ruler of the Kalingas, lying on the ground with his mighty arms adorned with angadas. Behold the ladies of Magadha, crying around their lord Jayatsena, their ornaments displaced, the long-eyed and sweet-voiced girls whose wails were stupefying her heart exceedingly, ladies worthy of costly beds lying now on the bare ground. Behold that bevy of fair ladies there; though tired with exertion and worn out with heat, beauty leaves not their forms, like the sightliness of the wreaths worn by the celestials though exposed to the sun, and their faces, through toil and the rays of the sun, look like faded lotuses. Behold the Kosala prince Brihadbala, his women plucking from his body the shafts with which Abhimanyu pierced him, losing their senses again and again.

There were the young sons of Dhrishtadyumna, of tender years, adorned with garlands of gold, fallen upon Drona like insects on a blazing fire, Drona whose car was a chamber of fire, his bow the flame and his shafts and darts and maces the fuel. And the five Kekaya brothers lay with their faces still turned toward the man who slew them, their coats of mail, of the splendour of heated gold, and their tall standards and cars and garlands, all of the same metal, shedding a bright light on the earth.

These wails, Gandhari said, were stupefying her heart exceedingly. And then she turned from the dead to the one who might have stopped it all. Since thou wert indifferent to the Kurus and the Pandavas whilst they slew each other, she said, therefore, O Govinda, thou shalt be the slayer of thy own kinsmen. In the thirty-sixth year from this day, thou shalt perish by disgusting means in the wilderness.

Krishna, the high-souled one, heard her out, and there was a faint smile on his face as he answered. There is none in the world, save myself, he said, that is capable of destroying the Vrishnis. Which was another way of saying that the end she spoke of was not something to be argued with or feared, for it was already written, and it would come from their own hands.

And so the curse was received, not resisted.
stories.reflection: Gandhari speaks from the raw center of grief, and her curse is grief given a shape and a date. Krishna does not defend himself or dispute the blame; he smiles, because he already knows how the Vrishnis will end, and he is not afraid of it.
stories.hero_scene: Gandhari standing among the slain on the field of Kurukshetra, pronouncing her curse upon Krishna, who receives it with a faint smile.
stories.variant_notes: Gandhari's curse; cf. mb_d_013 (the sages' curse).

stories.title: The Pigeon and the Hunter's Net
stories.story:
A pigeon built his nest in a forest tree, and there, with his mate, he raised a family. The two birds were bound to one another by a love that showed in everything they did. They were, in the way of birds, a single household, and the tree was their home.

They shared one bed and one seat. Where they roosted, they roosted together; where they walked, they walked side by side; what they said, they said to one another. They played together and ate together, and whatever one wanted, the other gave without being asked. It was a small life and a complete one, and they asked for nothing beyond it.

In time the hen laid her first eggs, and when the chicks hatched the two birds loved them with a tenderness that filled the nest with soft feathers and low, contented cooing. They fed them and kept them warm and watched over them, devoted to their children, and their days became nothing but the feeding and the keeping and the watching of those small, downy, open-beaked lives. The nest was all their world, and their world was warm.

The chicks grew, and their feathers came in soft as silk, and their cooing and their clumsy, innocent antics were the parents' whole delight. Watching them, the two birds felt that no harm could ever reach this tree, this nest, this small bright world they had made. Everything they had was in that nest — their young, their days, their whole reason for flying out and returning. They wanted for nothing, and they feared nothing, and they did not see the snare that their own tenderness was quietly weaving around them.

One day the two of them flew out together to gather food for the chicks. While they were gone, a hunter came through the forest, and he saw the young birds in the nest, alone and unguarded. He spread his net, and he caught them all.

The hen came home first. She saw her chicks struggling in the mesh, and love moved faster in her than fear. She did not pause, did not call out, did not think of herself. She flew straight into the net and settled down among her young. She did not try to pull them free; she only wanted to be with them.

Then the pigeon came home and saw them — his chicks, his mate, all of them tangled in the hunter's cords. He cried out: “Alas, what has my poor, misguided mind brought down upon us? My home is destroyed, my wife and children are caught — what use is my life now?” He could not bear to be the only one left free, to sit in an empty nest while those he loved were taken from him. Better, he thought, to share their fate than to outlive them in an empty home. The net that held them held everything he had. So he too flew into the net.

The hunter, finding them all gathered there for him, gathered them up and went on his way. And the nest stood empty in the tree, its soft lining stirring once in the wind and then going still. And so the very love that had made the nest a home became the thing that left it empty. The story was kept as a caution: a householder who clings to home and family as that bird did, bound to them and without peace, comes in the end to ruin — a human life, the one birth that stands with its door open to freedom, shut upon itself.
stories.reflection: The tale is offered as a warning, but it does not condemn love — it shows love without distance, a tenderness so total that it cannot let the lost stay lost. The pigeon is not wicked; he simply cannot bear to be the one left outside the net. What undoes him is not the hunter's cruelty but the completeness of his devotion.
stories.content_note: The pigeon and his family are caught in a hunter's net and do not survive.
stories.hero_scene: The pigeon flying deliberately into the hunter's net to join his mate and chicks, who are tangled in the mesh below, while the empty nest waits in the tree above.
visual_elements: a mood of tender love turning to grief

stories.title: Pingala the Courtesan's Renunciation
stories.story:
A wandering teacher, one of those who take their lessons from the world itself, used to say that among his teachers was a woman he had never met — a courtesan named Pingala, in the city of Videha. He spoke of her with the respect a student owes a teacher, for the lesson she had taught him had cost her a long and sleepless night.

Pingala lived by waiting. Each evening she dressed herself and adorned herself and went to the door of her house to wait for a man — a client, one who would come with money, for money was what she lived by. One night a man had promised to come to her, and so she stood at the door and watched the road. The evening fell, the lamps were lit along the street, and still he did not come. He had said he would come, but the street had emptied, and the road she watched stayed bare.

She waited, and she watched every man who passed, and with each approaching footstep her hope rose, and with each stranger who walked on by it fell. The night wore on. The lamps burned low, and the door grew cold against her shoulder. Her face grew thin and drawn, and her mind grew small and weary, and still she leaned in the doorway, holding herself together with nothing but the hope of a man who never came.

And then, in the dead of the night, something in her turned. It was not despair exactly — or if it was, it was the despair that sets a person free. She looked at herself leaning in that doorway, a woman dressed and waiting for a man who would not come, and she saw, with a sudden and terrible clarity, what she had been doing with her life, and for how many nights, and for how little.

“Look at the depth of my delusion,” she said to herself. “I have worn myself out for a man who brings a little money, when the giver of all joy, the one who grants every gift, is near me always, and I never once turned to him. What I have chased so wretchedly, let me give it up.” She saw, then, how needlessly she had tormented herself, night after night, for so small and passing a thing.

She looked down at the body she had dressed so carefully, and she saw it for what it was — a thing of bone and skin and hair, a house of nine doors that leaks and fills with what is foul. So much trouble, she thought, for a thing that would not last. And she wondered what she had been offering, and to whom, and why it had ever seemed worth a single sleepless night.

Then she cut off her hope — not the quiet hope of ordinary days, but the grasping, hungry hope that had kept her leaning at the door. She turned from the road, and she sat down, and the street that had held her eyes all night went dark and quiet behind her. and for the first time in longer than she could remember, she slept. And she slept in peace, the way a person sleeps when she owes no one anything.

The wandering teacher remembered her for this. A woman who had spent her nights waiting for what would not come, he said, had done in a single hour what the learned struggle a whole lifetime to do. And he kept her words as his own: that hope is the greatest of pains, and freedom from hope the greatest of joys.
stories.reflection: The story is careful not to make Pingala's peace a lesson for the poor or the lonely. What she gives up is not her life but her grasping — the hope that kept her leaning at a door for a man who never came, while the giver of every joy was, she realized, already near. Her “despair” is not a collapse but a release.
stories.hero_scene: Pingala leaning in her doorway in the lamplit night, watching the empty road, her face worn thin with waiting.
visual_elements: her face worn thin with waiting
a mood of longing giving way to peace

stories.title: The Yadava Fratricide at Prabhasa
stories.story:
Evening was coming down over the shore at Prabhasa, where the Yadavas had gathered to drink, and the sea lay calm beyond them. What came over them there had been waiting for them a long time. A brahmin's curse lay on the house: the day would come when the proud clan would turn on one another. Krishna knew it and had accepted it long ago. He did not stand in its way, for the hour had come.

They drank the maireya wine, and their minds were overthrown. As they drank, the destructive flame of dissension was kindled among them, and the proud heroes, their wits deranged, fell upon one another. Pradyumna turned on Samba, Akrura on Bhoja, Aniruddha on Satyaki; Gada and Sumitra and Suratha closed on one another, Subhadra on Sangramajit, and Nishatha and Ulmuka and Sahasrajit and Satajit and Bhanu. The Dasharhas and the Vrishnis and the Andhakas and the Bhojas and the Satvatas, all one family, forgot that they were one. Banners fell, and chariots and elephants careered into one another. Fathers fought sons, brothers fought brothers; sisters' sons and daughters' sons fell upon their uncles. Old friends who had once eaten from one plate fought one another.

There was a strangeness over it all. These were men who had grown up together and fought beside one another, and yet each now saw an enemy in the other's face. Some of them, in their madness, even took Balarama for an enemy. The wine was only part of it; something older and heavier was at work, completing itself, a veil drawn over their minds. And Krishna watched it without moving to stop it.

In the midst of the assembly, the drunken Satyaki laughed at Kritavarma and taunted him: what Kshatriya, he said, would slay men locked in the embraces of sleep, and therefore already dead? Then he rushed at Kritavarma and cut him down with a sword in the very sight of Krishna.

The quarrel spread through the whole clan. When their arrows were spent and their bows broke in their hands, they did not stop. They snatched up the eraka reeds that grew along the shore, innocent green things at the water's edge that no one had looked at twice, and in their hands the reeds became bars of iron, hard as thunderbolts, and they struck one another down with them. Son killed sire, and sire killed son. Uddhava, who watched it happen, remembered afterward how, as the sun went down, there had been among them a crushing of one another, like reeds.

Balarama took no part in any of it. He walked down to the ocean's edge, seated himself, entered into yoga, and there, quietly, he yielded up his body.

When the noise died, in a short time there was almost no one left alive of the Yadava race, only Krishna and his charioteer Daruka. The curse had run its course, and the sea kept its own counsel.
stories.reflection: The account offers no villain, only a doom arriving on time. What stays in the mind is the weapon: the reeds at their own feet, which become iron the moment they are taken up, as though the earth itself had been waiting to hand them the means.
stories.tradition_note: In the Mahabharata's telling, Krishna himself, seeing his son and the son of Sini slain, takes up a handful of the eraka grass and strikes down those before him. The Bhagavata Purana, followed here, keeps Krishna as witness and leaves only him and his charioteer alive.
stories.content_note: Kinsmen turn on one another and are destroyed; the violence is described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: One end remained, and a hunter's arrow was already on its way.
stories.hero_scene: Yadava warriors turning on one another along the shore at Prabhasa, seizing the eraka reeds that have become iron clubs, while Balarama sits apart at the ocean's edge in deep meditation.
visual_elements: eraka reeds turning to iron clubs

stories.title: The Hunter Jara Shoots Krishna's Foot
stories.story:
After the Yadavas were gone, a great silence lay over the shore, and Krishna walked into a forest near the sea and sat down alone. He had watched Balarama depart, and had seen the last of his people fall, and there was no one left to stay for. The forest was quiet around him, and the sea lay somewhere beyond the trees. At the foot of a pippala tree he seated himself, and there he sat in meditation, perfectly still, and let his own form change.

It was the form he did not often show: four-armed, bearing the Shrivatsa mark upon his chest, dark as a raincloud, bright with the splendour of molten gold. His face was a smiling lotus framed in dark curls. A waistband and a sacred thread, a diadem and bracelets and armlets adorned him, a garland of forest flowers lay about his body, and his own weapons, embodied, stood about him. He drew his right foot up upon his thigh and rested there, quiet, as if he had come to the end of a long road.

Not far off, an iron arrowhead carried a long story. Long before, an iron club had come into being in the Yadava house, a doom made into metal and foretold to crush the whole race. It had been ground to dust and thrown into the sea, so that its power might be scattered, but the sea gave the dust back as rushes along the shore. And now the last fragment of that iron, fashioned into a blade, sat on the shaft of a hunter who had come into the forest in search of deer.

His name was Jara. From a distance he saw Krishna's foot, and he mistook it for the face of a deer. He loosed the arrow, and it lodged in the sole.

He ran forward quickly to claim his prey, and he saw what he had done. A four-armed Lord sat there, radiant, and the terror of it took hold of him. He fell at Krishna's feet and begged forgiveness: this was done unknowingly, he said, in sin; let the sin of this deer-hunting sinner be swiftly destroyed, for the remembrance of that name destroys the darkness of ignorance in men. What he had pierced, the hunter understood, was a form that even Brahma and Rudra and the lords of speech could not fully know, and what could a man of worthless refuge say of such a thing?

And Krishna forgave him, and spoke to him gently, and raised him up. Then, quietly, the Lord relinquished his mortal body, and was gathered back into his own abode.

So it ended the way it had been written: not on a battlefield, but beneath a tree, by an arrow meant for a deer, loosed by a man who meant no harm and asked only to be forgiven.
stories.reflection: The arrow that ends Krishna's earthly form is forged from the last fragment of the iron that destroyed his people, so that one doom gathers up its own loose ends. A hunter who meant no harm becomes the instrument, and is forgiven, a strange and gentle close to a life spent in the middle of wars.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata describes Krishna lying on the earth in high yoga, pierced at the heel; the Bhagavata Purana, followed here, has him seated at the foot of a pippala tree with his foot drawn up.
stories.content_note: Krishna's earthly form is pierced by an arrow and he departs; the death is described gently.
stories.hero_scene: The four-armed Krishna seated in meditation at the foot of a pippala tree, his right foot drawn up, while the hunter Jara, bow in hand, stands frozen in terror at the edge of the forest.
stories.variant_notes: Vishnu Purana (5.37) condenses the shooting with the forgiveness and departure.

stories.title: Bhrigu Tests the Three Gods
stories.story:
Which of the three gods was greatest? The sages who gathered to debate it could not agree, and argument after argument came to nothing. It was, they thought, a fair test — for a god who could not bear a slight was, in the end, no greater than the man who offered it. At last they resolved to settle the matter not with words but with a test. They chose a tester, the sage Bhrigu, and sent him out with a single instruction: offer no bow, no hymn, no word of honor to any of the three, and watch what happened. A god's greatness, they reasoned, would show most clearly in how he bore an insult.

Bhrigu went first to Brahmaloka, the heaven of Brahma the creator — who happened to be his own father. He walked in and stood before the god and said nothing. No prostration, no praise, not a single syllable of respect. Brahma felt the anger rise in him, hot and gathering, ready to pour out. Then he looked at the man standing silent before him, his own son, and he held it down. He swallowed his anger and let the insult pass unanswered.

Next Bhrigu climbed to Kailasa, the mountain home of Shiva. Again he offered nothing: no greeting, no honor, no sign that he stood before a god at all. Shiva's anger did not wait to be held. It rose at once, and his trident was already lifting to strike when the goddess, his consort, threw herself at his feet and spoke soft words to him, and slowly the storm in him went still.

Last of all, Bhrigu came to Vaikuntha, the home of Vishnu. There he found the god lying at ease, the goddess of fortune resting against his chest. Bhrigu walked straight up to him and, without a word, drove his foot into that chest.

What happened next is the whole point of the story. Vishnu rose at once from his couch — not to strike back, but to bow. He bent his head to the sage and asked his forgiveness. Let the touch of the sage's foot purify me, he said, and all who depend upon me. “Today,” he went on, “your foot has made me the true dwelling of Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune who rests upon this chest.”

Bhrigu stood silent. This was not the answer he had come prepared to receive, and it undid him. He had expected, at best, a god who could master his temper. He had found instead a god who seemed not to have one — who met a blow not with patience but with welcome, as though the foot that struck him had come bearing a gift.

He returned to the assembly of sages and told them what he had seen, and they listened in wonder, and the doubt they had carried fell away. In Vishnu, they saw now, dwelt all that a soul could want of a god — righteousness, and wisdom, and the freedom from desire, and a nature so pure that it could not be provoked. Greatness, Bhrigu told them, does not live in the power to punish an insult. It lives in the one who can take a blow and answer it with calm. Of the three, only Vishnu had met rage with stillness and a kick with a blessing; only Vishnu was the true abode of peace and of fearlessness.

And so the question was answered — not by the one who raged, not by the one who merely mastered his rage, but by the one in whom no rage rose at all.
stories.reflection: The sages set out to measure power and instead measured restraint. Two gods burned at an insult; the third apologized to the foot that struck him — and that, Bhrigu reported back, is where greatness actually lives. The test was meant to find strength, and it found the thing that most looks like weakness: the man who does not hit back.
